Pulcinella. A one-act ballet choreographed by Léonide Massine in 1920 for the Ballets Russes, with music by Igor Stravinsky adapted from eighteenth-century Italian composers, primarily Pergolesi. The work is a lighthearted comedy rooted in commedia dell'arte, featuring the stock character Pulcinella, a resourceful servant, and his romantic entanglements. It combines Stravinsky's witty neo-classical score with Massine's comic choreography and traditional masked-character conventions.

Stravinsky based his score on fragments by Pergolesi and other Italian masters, creating a neo-classical work that playfully reinvents Baroque material with twentieth-century dissonance and humor. Léonide Massine choreographed the work and danced the title role, bringing slapstick comedy and detailed characterization to classical ballet form. Massine was famous for blending mime, character work, and virtuosity.

The plot is a traditional commedia dell'arte scenario: Pulcinella, a cunning servant, engages in romantic intrigue with multiple characters while using disguises and tricks to escape trouble and win the day. The character of Pulcinella wears the iconic white costume and black mask of the traditional stock character, grounding the ballet in theatrical tradition.

The ensemble features other commedia archetypes: lovers, soldiers, and servants engaged in farcical complications and synchronized ensemble dances that parody classical ballet forms. The score features moments of mock-heroic orchestration and abrupt tonal shifts, reflecting Stravinsky's neo-classical aesthetic of playful subversion.

Pulcinella premiered at the Paris Opéra on 15 May 1920 and demonstrated Stravinsky's ability to reinvent historical material while establishing Massine as a master of character choreography. The work connects to Stravinsky, the composer who created the neo-classical, witty score, and to Massine, the choreographer-dancer who established the character-dance tradition in ballet.
